h1:
Waterfalls Around Chaiyaphum
Tat Ton, Tat Fa, Thep Prathan + Rainy-Season Swimming Spots
intro: Chaiyaphum hides waterfalls across several national parks — from Tat Ton, the closest one to town, to Tat Fa, which works like a natural rock slide, and the falls inside Pa Hin Ngam and Sai Thong that pair perfectly with the krachiao flower fields. The rainy season brings the most water and the prettiest views, but it's also when you have to watch out for flash floods. Here are the waterfalls you can actually visit right now, with swimming spots, entry fees and opening hours.

blocks.html: When it comes to nature trips around Chaiyaphum, waterfalls are the reason people drive out of town. The rainy season (roughly June to October) is when the water is highest and the falls look their best — green rock terraces, clear pools you can actually wade into. Some are barely 20-odd kilometres from town; others sit deep inside the parks up on the Phanghoei range, right where the krachiao flower fields bloom. We've ordered them from closest to town outward, to make planning a route easier.

blocks.text: Tat Ton Waterfall — Closest to Town, Swimmable Year-Round

blocks.html: Tat Ton Waterfall sits inside Tat Ton National Park, about 21 kilometres from Chaiyaphum town. It's the one locals visit most often because it's close and has water flowing almost all year. The top is a wide rock platform around 50 metres across, running about 300 metres along the stream with big shady trees on both banks. The water slides down the rock and drops over a cliff about 6 metres high, spanning the full 50-metre width — in the rainy season the whole cliff turns into a curtain of water.

items: Distance — about 21 km from Chaiyaphum town, roughly a 30-minute drive on good road the whole way
Entry (Thai rate) — adults 40 THB, children 20 THB, car around 30 THB
Swimming spots — you can swim in the pools on the rock platform above the falls; pick a spot the rangers allow where the water isn't deep

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.html: Tat Ton is best in the morning before the crowds. On long weekends locals fill the rock platform with picnic mats. If you want it quiet, come on a weekday or before 10am.

blocks.text: Tat Fa Waterfall — A Natural Rock Slide

blocks.html: Tat Fa Waterfall is also within Tat Ton National Park, but about 18 kilometres east of the park headquarters, in the Ban Na Wang area of Na Siao subdistrict. What sets Tat Fa apart is its surface: the rock is fairly smooth and slanted with few ledges, so the water slides across the whole width like a long natural slide. It's especially full in the rainy season — the sheet of water across the cliff looks far better than in the dry months.

items: Location — inside Tat Ton National Park, about 18 km east of the park headquarters; the last stretch is a narrow road, so ask the rangers for directions first
Best time — the rainy season, when water fills the cliff and you see a sheet of water sliding across the whole rock face
Watch out — the rock is very smooth and slippery; take care walking on it and wear rubber shoes with grippy soles

blocks.text: Thep Prathan Waterfall — Just Before Pa Hin Ngam

blocks.html: Thep Prathan Waterfall is in Ban Rai subdistrict, Thep Sathit district — a medium-sized fall surrounded by intact forest, about 7 kilometres before you reach Pa Hin Ngam National Park. It's fairly flat, with big boulders forming a wide platform that steps down in low tiers. It makes a good stop on the way up to Pa Hin Ngam or the krachiao flower fields.

blocks.title: Make the route count
blocks.html: Thep Prathan sits right on the road up to Pa Hin Ngam. Stop at the waterfall in the morning, then carry on up to see the krachiao flower fields and the Lan Hin Ngam rock field — all easily done in the same day.

blocks.text: Sai Thong & Chuan Chom Falls — Inside Sai Thong National Park

blocks.html: Sai Thong National Park covers the Phanghoei range across Nong Bua Rawe, Thep Sathit, Phakdi Chumphon and Nong Bua Daeng districts — a large stretch of forest with both waterfalls and krachiao flower fields (here called the Bua Sawan fields). Early in the rainy season, the main waterfall has two tiers you can walk between.

items.name: Sai Thong Waterfall (Wang Sai)
items.blurb: The fall itself is about 5 metres high, with a large pool below it called Wang Sai where you can swim. Above it is another big pool called Wang Ngueak, with the stream winding down the rock platform for about 150 metres.
items.meta: Swim at Wang Sai · fullest in the rains

items.name: Chuan Chom Waterfall
items.blurb: About 2 kilometres above Sai Thong along the nature trail, around 20 metres high and 50 metres wide, set under thick shade. This tier is taller and fuller, good for anyone who likes a short forest walk.
items.meta: ~2 km up from Sai Thong · 20 m high

blocks.html: Sai Thong stands out because you can pair it with the Pha Sawan and Pha Ham Hot viewpoints and the krachiao flower fields on a single trip. Plan it for early in the rains and you'll get both full waterfalls and the krachiao in bloom at the same time.

blocks.title: The krachiao fields only bloom in the rains
blocks.html: The krachiao flower fields at Sai Thong and Pa Hin Ngam bloom only in the rainy season, roughly June to August, and the peak shifts from year to year. Before you go, check the park's Facebook page or hotline so you don't arrive to a field that hasn't bloomed yet or has already faded.

blocks.text: Full in the Rains — but Watch for Flash Floods

blocks.html: The rainy season is when Chaiyaphum's waterfalls look their best, but it's also when flash floods are the biggest risk. Floodwater comes fast and hard, sometimes when the sky right above the waterfall isn't even raining. Before you get in, always read the signs and listen to ranger announcements first.

items: Watch the water level and colour — if it starts turning muddy red or you see branches and leaves floating down, get out immediately; that's a sign a flash flood is coming
Only swim where the rangers allow it; don't climb over above the falls or get into pools deeper than you can handle
Rock platforms are very slippery in the rains — wear rubber shoes with grippy soles, not flat-soled flip-flops
Keep valuables in a waterproof bag, and never leave small children to swim alone
Leave the park before dark — the forest roads have no lights and rain makes visibility poor

blocks.html: With two days you can cover both the falls near town and the ones deep in the forest. Splitting the zones across separate days makes for easier driving, since Pa Hin Ngam and Sai Thong are in a different direction from Tat Ton.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Near-Town Zone — Tat Ton + Tat Fa

items.activity: Arrive at Tat Ton Waterfall and swim in the upper rock pools while it's still quiet
Carry on to Tat Fa Waterfall in the same park to see the natural rock slide
items.note: Ask the rangers for directions first

items.activity: Head back into town for lunch and rest through the afternoon heat
Walk to the Phaya Lae monument / evening market in town
items.note: An easy way to close the day

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Deep-Forest Zone — Thep Prathan + Sai Thong / Pa Hin Ngam

items.activity: Leave town for Thep Sathit district (a long drive — allow extra time)
Stop at Thep Prathan Waterfall before reaching Pa Hin Ngam
Enter Pa Hin Ngam or Sai Thong for the waterfall + krachiao flower fields (if in bloom)
items.note: Check the bloom window before you go

items.activity: Walk to Sai Thong–Chuan Chom falls if you still have energy, then head back before dark

faq.q: Which Chaiyaphum waterfall is closest to town?
faq.a: Tat Ton Waterfall in Tat Ton National Park, about 21 kilometres from town — roughly a 30-minute drive. It has water flowing almost all year and you can swim in the pools on the rock platform. Open daily 08.00–18.00.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Chaiyaphum's waterfalls?
faq.a: The rainy season, around June to October, when the water is highest and the falls look their best. If you also want the krachiao flower fields, aim for early in the rains (about June to August), but check the bloom window with the park first, since the peak shifts each year.

faq.q: Is it safe to swim at Chaiyaphum's waterfalls in the rainy season?
faq.a: You can, as long as you pick a spot the rangers allow where the water isn't deep — but watch out for flash floods, which come fast and hard. If the water starts turning muddy red or you see branches floating down, get out immediately, and don't climb over above the falls.

faq.q: How much is entry to Chaiyaphum's waterfall parks?
faq.a: The parks charge Thai visitors around 40 THB for adults and 20 THB for children, plus about 30 THB for a car. Foreign visitors pay more. Prices may change according to each park's notices.

faq.q: What's the difference between Sai Thong and Chuan Chom falls?
faq.a: Sai Thong Waterfall (Wang Sai) is about 5 metres high with a large pool you can swim in. Chuan Chom Waterfall is about 2 kilometres farther up along the nature trail, around 20 metres high — taller and fuller, but you have to walk in to reach it.
